Who do the School’s researchers publish with, and how has this changed? This page classifies the
5,226 Scopus records from 1981 to the export of
2 November 2026 by the institutions in their affiliations: AUTH alone, possibly several of its
units (single-institution), AUTH with other organisations in Greece only (national), or with
at least one affiliation abroad (international). As in the usual bibliometric indicators, every
affiliation counts, including a second affiliation that an SECE author holds at another institution (a
joint, adjunct or visiting position); where this changes the reading, the page also gives the
external-partner value, counting only affiliations of co-authors who are not SECE authors. Partner
institutions are identified by matching the affiliations to the Research Organization Registry (ROR).
2026 is a partial year: the yearly counts show it marked, and it is left out of the shares by
year and period, trends and averages. Partner countries are covered in 

Global reach.



Key findings

International co-authorship more than doubled, from 21.7% of the papers in
2001–2005 to 50.6% in 2021–2025, and was
56.9% in 2025. Counting only affiliations of co-authors who
are not SECE authors, the shares are 20.0%,
46.7% and 53.2%:
50 of the 649 international
papers of 2021–2025 and 11 of the
169 of 2025 are international only through SECE
authors’ own second affiliations abroad. Papers with AUTH as the only institution fell from
50.5% to 26.3%.

Since 1981 the School has published with 810 partner
institutions. The Centre for Research and Technology Hellas (CERTH) with its Information Technologies
Institute (ITI) appears on 371 papers, more than any other partner; ROR
lists ITI as an organisation of its own, so the ranking of partner institutions is led by
Khalifa University (280 papers), CERTH's Information Technologies Institute (265) and the University of Western Macedonia (247). Some of these links come from SECE authors who hold a
position at the partner institution: 93 of the 280 papers with Khalifa University and 61 of the 265 with CERTH's Information Technologies Institute link to the institution only through SECE authors’ own second affiliations, and so do most of the 96 papers with the Lebanese American University; counting only affiliations of co-authors
who are not SECE authors, the University of Western Macedonia ranks first,
with 232 papers.

Universities account for the growth: 63.7% of the
2021–2025 papers had a university partner, against
32.8% in 2001–2005. Companies listed in ROR
appear on only 3.3% of the recent papers; counting also
companies outside ROR, recognised by their legal form, 11.5%
(3.1% in 2001–2005).

Within Greece, the University of Western Macedonia (109 papers)
and the Democritus University of Thrace (67) were the most
frequent partners in 2021–2025; CERTH with ITI peaked in 2006–2010
(104 papers, 75
counting only affiliations of co-authors who are not SECE authors) and had
51 in 2021–2025, nearly all of them with co-authors from CERTH or ITI who are not SECE authors.

The partner network widened: 140.0 distinct partner institutions
a year in 2021–2025 against 30.2 in 2001–2005
(4.6 times as many), ahead of the
4.0-fold growth in papers with a matched partner institution.

Figure 1:Share of papers by collaboration type, 1995–2025 (number of papers in
the hover). The international bars have two parts: the hatched part counts the papers that are
international only through SECE authors’ own second affiliations abroad, and the solid part is the
external-partner share, counting only affiliations of co-authors who are not SECE authors.
Where the hatched part would rest on fewer than 3 SECE authors, or would let such a
part be worked out from other values on this site (such as the totals of 

Table 1), the
international bar is dotted and not split. 2026 (partial year) is not shown. Earlier years, with at most
29 papers a year, are included in 

Table 1.

Working with other institutions has become the norm (

Figure 1). In
2001–2005, 50.5% of the School’s papers listed no institution
other than AUTH; in 2021–2025 the share was 26.3%. International
co-authorship rose from 21.7% to 50.6% of the
papers over the same twenty years and was 56.9% in 2025, after a high of 57.2% in 2024; the external-partner share rose
from 20.0% to 46.7% and
reached 53.2% in 2025, its highest of any full year. The difference between the
two grew from 1.7 percentage points in 2001–2005 to
3.9 in 2021–2025 (3.7 in
2025): 8 of the 104
international papers of 2001–2005, 50 of the
649 of 2021–2025 and 11
of the 169 of 2025 are international only through
SECE authors’ own second affiliations abroad. The national share (partners in Greece only) has stayed
between 20.0% and 28.0% in every period since 2001–2005: from
2001–2005 to 2021–2025 the international share gained 28.9
percentage points and the national share lost 4.7
(26.6 and 1.3 on the
external-partner basis), so the move away from single-institution papers went entirely to
international collaboration.
Greek partners did not lose ground: counting also the international papers that include one,
40.2% of the 2021–2025 papers had a partner affiliation in Greece
outside AUTH, against 37.4% in 2001–2005. How the collaboration
types differ in citations is shown in 

Citation impact.

Table 1:Collaboration types by five-year period: number of papers and share of each type (full years only). In
brackets, where it differs: the external-partner share, counting only affiliations of co-authors who are
not SECE authors; a dash where it is not shown, because the difference would rest on fewer than
3 SECE authors or would let such a difference be worked out, also with values on other
pages (see the notes).

Table 1 gives both bases by period. Over all years
(1981–2026), counting only affiliations of co-authors who are not SECE
authors gives 2,308 single-institution,
1,062 national and 1,856
international papers, against 2,140,
1,133 and 1,953 when every
affiliation counts. Of the international papers,
97 are international only through SECE authors’ own second affiliations
abroad (65 become single-institution and 32
national), and 103 national papers become single-institution because all
their affiliations outside AUTH are SECE authors’ own second affiliations.

A partner institution is the top-level ROR organisation behind an affiliation outside AUTH: a
university, research centre, hospital, company or public body. Institutes and hospitals that ROR places
under a parent organisation count under the parent; universities count on their own, even within a
university system. Since 1981, SECE papers have involved
810 distinct partner institutions, 74 of them
in Greece and 735 abroad; 1 foreign institution appears only through a campus or branch in Greece. Counting only
affiliations of co-authors who are not SECE authors, 805 remain
(730 abroad); the other 5
appear only through SECE authors’ own second affiliations.

Figure 2:The 26 most frequent partner institutions (43 papers
or more), 1981–2026 (2026 to 2 November 2026):
papers with at least one affiliation of the institution,
coloured by sector (primary ROR type). The hatched end of a bar counts the papers that link to the
institution only through SECE authors’ own second affiliations, and an asterisk marks the institutions
where these are at least half of the papers; where fewer than 3 SECE authors hold
these affiliations, or the number would let such a count be worked out, it is not shown and the bar has no
hatched end. The hover shows the
location, these counts, the number of papers in 2021–2025 and the year of the first joint paper.

Of the 26 institutions in 

Figure 2, 15
are Greek. The
list is led by Khalifa University, ahead of CERTH’s Information Technologies Institute
(ITI), which ROR records as an organisation of its own; ITI appears on
265 papers, the rest of CERTH on
111 and CERTH as a whole on 371,
more than any other partner. The most frequent partners abroad are
Khalifa University (280 papers), the University of Huddersfield (128) and the Lebanese American University (96, most of them only through SECE authors’ own second affiliations). Paper counts measure
co-authorship, not formal agreements, and one long-running joint project can produce many joint papers.
Some links also come from SECE authors who hold a position at the partner institution:
93 of the 280 papers with Khalifa University, 61 of the 265 with CERTH's Information Technologies Institute and 24 of the 111 with the Centre for Research and Technology Hellas link to the institution only through SECE authors’ own second affiliations, and so do most of the 96 papers with the Lebanese American University. Counting only affiliations of co-authors who are not
SECE authors, the ranking would be led by the University of Western Macedonia (232 papers), CERTH's Information Technologies Institute (204) and Khalifa University (187).

Figure 3:The 15 most frequent partner institutions in 2021–2025, the latest five
full years (25 papers or more), coloured by sector; hatching and asterisks as in


Figure 2.

In 2021–2025 the most frequent partners were
Khalifa University (122 papers), the University of Western Macedonia (109), the Lebanese American University (89, most of them only through SECE authors’ own second affiliations) and the University of Huddersfield (82) (

Figure 3);
6 of the 15 are outside Greece. Counting only affiliations of co-authors
who are not SECE authors, the four most frequent were the University of Western Macedonia, Khalifa University, the University of Huddersfield and the Democritus University of Thrace.
The network has a long tail: 41.1% of all partner institutions appear on a
single paper and 107 on ten or more, while the 11 most
frequent partners, with 82 papers or more each, together appear on
50.0% of the 2,898 papers with a matched partner
institution.

Each partner institution takes its primary ROR type as its sector (see


Methodology & data): education (universities and colleges), research facility,
nonprofit, government, company and healthcare.

Figure 4:Share of papers with at least one partner institution of each sector, in three-year windows (each
year with the two before it), 1997–2025; 2026 is
left out. Each panel has its own vertical scale. A paper can count in several sectors.

Universities account for almost all of the growth in collaboration (

Figure 4):
63.7% of the 2021–2025 papers had at least one
university partner, against 32.8% in 2001–2005.
The other sectors each appear on a small share of the papers. Research facilities went from
7.5% to 6.9%
over the same periods, government bodies from 3.1% to
3.0% and hospitals from
0.2% to 1.9%.
The nonprofit panel is shaped by ITI, which ROR types as nonprofit (CERTH itself is a research
facility): ITI is on 59 of the 62
papers with a nonprofit partner in 2001–2005, but on only 29 of
the 85 in 2021–2025. Companies are discussed below.

Figure 5:Share of papers with at least one company among the partner institutions, by five-year period (labels:
both kinds together). The bars separate companies listed in ROR (the definition used on the other pages)
from companies outside ROR, recognised by a legal form (S.A., Ltd, GmbH, Inc., SpA, B.V., P.C. and
similar) in an unmatched affiliation; the labels give both together.

Industry co-authorship is small. Companies listed in ROR appear on
3.3% of the 2021–2025 papers, against
2.1% in 2001–2005; the most frequent since
1981 are ABB (26 papers), the Hellenic Telecommunications Organization (16) and Intracom Telecom (13, most of them only through SECE authors’ own second affiliations). ROR lists few
companies, especially small ones: 183 of the
668 distinct unmatched affiliations outside AUTH name a company by its
legal form,
57.9% of them with an address in Greece. Counting these companies too, industry
co-authorship rose from 3.1% of the papers in
2001–2005 to 11.5%
(148 papers) in 2021–2025
(

Figure 5), mostly with companies outside ROR. Part of this rise may reflect how
affiliations are written rather than more industry links, and companies named without a legal form are
still missed.

Figure 6:The 15 most frequent Greek partner institutions: papers by five-year period (the years before
2001 together), with the total for 1981–2025 on the right. Names are
shortened (CERTH-ITI: CERTH’s Information Technologies Institute; NTUA, NKUA: the National Technical and
the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens; TEI: technological educational institute); the hover
gives the full names.
2026 (partial) is not included.

The 74 Greek partner institutions have changed places over time
(

Figure 6). CERTH with its ITI was the main Greek partner in the 2000s and peaked in
2006–2010 (104 papers, or
75 counting only affiliations of co-authors who are not SECE
authors); in 2021–2025 it appeared on
51, nearly all of them with co-authors from CERTH or ITI who are not SECE authors, so part of the decline comes from fewer papers on which
CERTH or ITI appears only through SECE authors’ own second affiliations. The most frequent Greek partners
of 2021–2025 were the University of Western Macedonia (109
papers, up from 32 in 2011–2015) and the Democritus University of Thrace
(67, up from
11). Local partners weigh heavily: institutions based in
Thessaloniki appear on 37.6% of the 1,562
papers with a matched Greek partner institution. Part of the change is administrative: the
technological educational institutes (TEIs) were merged into universities in 2018–2019, so, for
example, papers with the Alexander TEI of Thessaloniki give way to papers with the International
Hellenic University.

Figure 7:Distinct partner institutions per year, 1995–2026: first-time partners
(first joint paper in the data, which start in 1981) and returning partners.
2026 is partial (records to 2 November 2026).

The partner network has widened (

Figure 7). Papers of 2021–2025 involved
140.0 distinct partner institutions a year on average,
4.6 times the 30.2 of 2001–2005.
This rise was ahead of the 4.0-fold growth in papers with a matched
partner institution (44.4 to 178.4 a
year), so the ratio of distinct partners to papers with a partner rose from
0.68 to 0.78; total output grew
2.7 times. The inflow of new partners eased from
39.0 first-time partners a year in 2016–2020 to
36.6 in 2021–2025 (13.2 in
2001–2005); the most in a single full year was 55, in
2025.

Figure 8:Papers by number of partner institutions, by five-year period, 1996–2000 to
2021–2025 (full years only). None: no matched partner institution, mostly single-institution
papers.

Papers increasingly involve several partner institutions (

Figure 8). Papers
with two or more rose from 15.2% of the output in 2001–2005
to 37.6% in 2021–2025, and papers without a matched partner
fell from 53.7% to 30.5%. The mean
number of partner institutions per paper went from 0.69 to
1.50; the most on a single paper is
27, on a paper of 2026.

Affiliations, not people. Collaboration types and partners come from the affiliations listed on
each record. A paper is international when at least one affiliation is outside Greece (unmatched
strings count through the country they name), national when it has a partner affiliation in Greece
and none abroad, and single-institution otherwise; 

Methodology & data gives the
full definitions. This address-based rule is the usual one (SciVal and the Leiden Ranking, for
example, count international collaboration from the countries in the affiliations), and it counts every
affiliation, including a second affiliation that an SECE author holds abroad or at another Greek
institution.

SECE authors’ own second affiliations. Scopus also lists the affiliations of each author, so an
affiliation outside AUTH counts as an SECE author’s own when every author of the paper who lists it is an
SECE author (an author whose own affiliation names the School). There are
534 such affiliations on 475 papers:
325 abroad, 199 in Greece and
10 without a recognisable country; every affiliation on the records is listed by at least one of their authors. Counting only
affiliations of co-authors who are not SECE authors, 97 of the
1,953 international papers (5.0%)
are not international and 103 of the
1,133 national papers (9.1%)
become single-institution (

Table 1 gives the shares by period). Most other figures
on this page change little: in 2021–2025, for example, 61.2% of the
papers have a university partner on that basis (63.7%
counting every affiliation), and a paper has 1.37 partner
institutions on average (1.50).

Small groups. No number of papers that link to an institution, a sector or a collaboration type only
through SECE authors’ own second affiliations is shown, in any year or period, unless it is zero or at least
3 SECE authors hold these affiliations, since with fewer it would in practice be one or
two people’s paper count. This also covers numbers that could be worked out from others, on this page or
with the values of other pages, such as the difference between the two bases or a total minus its shown
parts: such values are left out or described in words, the bars concerned have no hatched end
(

Figure 2, 

Figure 3) or no split (

Figure 1), and


Table 1 shows a dash instead of the external-partner share.

Matching coverage. Partner institutions require a match to ROR. Of the affiliation occurrences,
94.1% were matched overall and 89.1% outside AUTH
(86.7% of the distinct strings outside AUTH);
188 of the 3,086 national or international
papers have no matched partner institution at all. Institution counts are therefore lower bounds.
Coverage outside AUTH is similar in 2001–2005 (86.7%) and
2021–2025 (87.3%) and lower before 2001
(72.1% in 1996–2000), so comparisons of partner
institutions between 2001–2005 and 2021–2025 are not driven by a change in overall matching
coverage. Companies are the exception: ROR lists few of them, and
10 of the
15 papers with a company partner in 2001–2005
had a company listed in ROR, but only 42 of the
148 in 2021–2025 (

Figure 5).
The collaboration types depend much less on the matching, because they also
use the country and the institution named in each affiliation. The accuracy of the matching is
reported in 

Methodology & data.

Institutions as ROR records them. ROR v2.15 lists CERTH’s Information Technologies Institute
without a parent, so ITI (265 papers) and the rest of CERTH
(111) are counted as two institutions here and on the other
pages. Former TEIs follow ROR too: some are records of their own (such as the Alexander TEI of
Thessaloniki), others are recorded as predecessors of the university that absorbed them (the TEI of
Western Macedonia counts as the University of Western Macedonia).

Sectors are primary ROR types, which can be coarse: national research organisations, for
example, are typed government or nonprofit depending on the record. Partners of type archive or other
(on 23 papers) are not shown in 

Figure 4.

Companies. The legal-form rule adds companies that ROR lacks but misses companies named without a
legal form, so industry co-authorship is probably still understated. The site-wide industry flag
(used in 

Citation impact) counts only companies listed in ROR.

Counts are full counts: a paper counts once for every partner institution, sector and type it
involves. 2026 is partial (records to 2 November 2026) and is left out of periods,
of the shares by year and period and of averages; totals over all years include it.

This page looks at how much of the School’s research acknowledges external funding, which funders
appear most often, how the mix of funders has changed and how much of the output is openly accessible.
It draws on two fields of the 5,226 Scopus records: the funding details that Scopus
extracts from the acknowledgements of the papers (5,540 funder entries on
1,936 publications) and the open-access flags, which describe the status of each
publication on 2 November 2026. A publication counts as funded when Scopus lists at least one funder for
it; funder names were normalised and sorted into groups (see the notes at the end). 2026 is
a partial year: its records count in the funder totals but are left out of all shares, by year and by
period, and of the comparisons.



Key findings

66.0% of the publications of 2021–2025 acknowledge at least one
funder, against 18.2% in 2011–2015. The largest one-year rise since
2001 came in 2018, from 27.6% to
47.0%, and was concentrated in EU and Greek public funding;
part of it may reflect more complete indexing of acknowledgements by Scopus.

The EU is the most frequent source of funding: 40.3% of the
2021–2025 publications acknowledge it, 28.4% through EU research
programmes and 14.7% through EU structural and recovery funds.
Horizon 2020 is the most frequently acknowledged funder (331
publications).

HFRI, first acknowledged in 2018, is now the most frequently acknowledged Greek public
funder: 147 publications of 2021–2025 acknowledge it. GSRT was
acknowledged by 50 publications of 2006–2010, but already by only
10 in 2011–2015 and by 9 in
2021–2025.

42.5% of the 2021–2025 publications are open access, against
12.5% in 2011–2015; gold is the main route
(20.0%). Journal publications are open far more often
(61.6%) than conference papers (18.5%).

Funded journal publications of 2021–2025 are open access more often than unfunded ones
(65.7% against
54.4%), and those acknowledging an EU research programme
most often (78.2%).

Figure 1:Share of publications with at least one funding acknowledgement in Scopus, by year, for all publications
and by source type (numbers in the hover). 2026 (partial year) is not
shown.

The share of publications with a funding acknowledgement stayed below a fifth in 2001–2005, 2006–2010 and 2011–2015
(14.8%, 17.7% and 18.2%), then rose to 43.8% in 2016–2020 and
66.0% in 2021–2025 (

Figure 1). Conference papers
changed most: 8.7% of them acknowledged funding in 2011–2015 and
70.6% in 2021–2025, when they did so more often than journal
publications (64.1%).

In 2018, the year with the largest increase since 2001, the share rose in journal
publications (36.3% to 53.3%) and conference papers
(19.6% to 47.3%) alike. A step of this size within one year
may partly reflect more complete indexing of acknowledgements by Scopus, but it is concentrated in EU and
Greek public funding: the share of publications acknowledging EU or Greek public funders rose from
13.2% to
34.3%, while the share acknowledging other public funders
(those of other countries and international bodies) fell slightly, from 13.2% to 11.6%.
New Greek funders appear in the same year: the funding agency HFRI and the RESEARCH – CREATE – INNOVATE action are both first acknowledged in 2018.

The chart starts in 2001: from that five-year period on, the School published at least
50 papers every year, so that yearly shares do not rest on a handful of papers.
Scopus lists funders for 73 of the 422 earlier
publications, the first from 1989. The data show no break in coverage around 2008:
16.3% of the publications of 2001–2007 and
17.8% of those of 2008–2015 have funding details.

Figure 2:The 20 most frequently acknowledged funders, 1981–2026:
publications that acknowledge each funder, coloured by funder group (hover: publications of
2021–2025 and years with acknowledgements). Names are normalised, and a few bars combine closely
related bodies, such as the successive Greek ministries or the framework programmes before FP7. A
publication can acknowledge several funders.

Horizon 2020 heads the list (331 publications), followed by
the Greek programmes co-financed by EU structural funds (NSRF/ESPA, 205), the European Social Fund (186), HFRI (177) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC, 151) (

Figure 2). Of the 20 funders,
10 are EU programmes or funds and 4 are Greek public bodies. The
ranking has changed over time: GSRT was acknowledged by 50 publications in
2006–2010, 10 in 2011–2015, 11 in
2016–2020 and 9 in 2021–2025, while HFRI was acknowledged by
147 publications in 2021–2025.

Funders from abroad come with the School’s international links: all of the
290 publications that acknowledge the National Natural Science Foundation of China
(151), Khalifa University (92) or the
UK’s EPSRC (72) are international papers (have an affiliation abroad).
Counting only affiliations of co-authors who are not SECE authors, so that an SECE author's own second affiliation abroad does not count, almost all of them are still international; the few others, which acknowledge Khalifa University, have no affiliation abroad other than such second affiliations.

Figure 3:Share of the funded publications that acknowledge at least one funder in each group, by five-year
period, 2001–2025 (n = funded publications). A publication can count in
several groups, so the columns do not add up to 100%. 2026 is not shown (partial year).

EU research programmes are acknowledged by 43.0% of the funded
publications of 2021–2025 and EU structural and recovery funds by
22.2%; together, 61.0% of the
funded publications acknowledge EU funding (

Figure 3). Of the 2021–2025 publications with
EU structural or recovery funds, 37.2% name one of the Greek NSRF/ESPA programmes that
these funds co-finance.

The share of Greek public funders changed most. They appeared on
53.5% of the funded publications of 2006–2010
(77 publications), on 9.5% in
2016–2020 (46) and on 20.3%
in 2021–2025 (172). Their number grew
2.2 times from 2006–2010 to 2021–2025; the share fell because the
funded publications multiplied (144 to 847).
Other public funders (those of other countries, EU member states included, and international bodies) peaked
at 31.2% in 2016–2020;
93.8% of the publications acknowledging them in
1981–2025 are international papers (also when counting only affiliations of co-authors who are not SECE authors).
Universities and research centres reached 19.0% in 2021–2025
(67.1% of these publications acknowledge Khalifa University or AUTH’s own funds),
while industry (2.4%) and foundations
(4.1%) remain small.

Figure 4:Share of publications acknowledging EU funding, by year from 2001: EU research programmes (the
framework programmes
up to Horizon Europe, with the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions, the ERC and COST), EU structural and recovery
funds (ESF, ERDF, the NSRF/ESPA programmes co-financed by Greece, Interreg, NextGenerationEU) and either of
the two (numbers in the hover). 2026 (partial year) is not shown.

In 2021–2025, 40.3% of the publications acknowledged EU
funding, against 11.7% in 2011–2015 and
6.9% in 2001–2005; the highest yearly share was
50.3% in 2021 (

Figure 4). The two
kinds of EU funding followed different paths. Research programmes reached their highest share in
2024 (30.7%). Structural and recovery funds peaked
at 27.9% in 2020 and fell to 7.6% in 2024 (12.5% in 2025). Much of
the peak came from the
Greek RESEARCH – CREATE – INNOVATE action: it is acknowledged on 48.4% of the
2020 publications with EU structural funds, and on 100 publications in
all, from 2018 to 2024.

Figure 5:Share of publications that are open access, by route and year from 2001, as flagged by Scopus
on 2 November 2026.
Gold: published in a fully open-access journal; hybrid: open article in a subscription journal; bronze:
free to read on the publisher’s site without an open licence; green: only a repository copy is open. A
publication with several routes counts once, in the first route of this list. 2026
(partial year) is not shown.

Open access grew from 6.9% of the publications of 2001–2005 and
12.5% of those of 2011–2015 to 29.0% in
2016–2020 and 42.5% in 2021–2025; the highest yearly share was
45.2% in 2023 (

Figure 5). Gold is now
the main route (20.0% of the 2021–2025 publications), ahead
of green (12.5%), hybrid
(8.6%, up from 3.3% in
2016–2020) and bronze (1.4%).

The lower shares of the years after 2023 (40.0% in 2024 and 41.8% in 2025) are at least partly a
matter of timing: a repository copy is flagged for 40.2% of the
publications of 2021 but for 27.6% and 28.3% of those of 2024 and 2025.
Such copies often appear only after a publisher’s embargo, so the shares of the most
recent years are likely to rise in later snapshots.

Open access by source type and publisher

records.content:
Figure 6:Open-access share by route for the publications of 2021–2025: by source type (top) and, for
journal publications, by publisher (bottom: publishers with at least 15 journal
publications in these years). The number at the end of each bar is the share open by any route.
Publisher imprints are grouped as on the 

Venues & publishers page.

Journal publications are open far more often (61.6% in 2021–2025) than
conference papers (18.5%), which are open mostly through repository
copies: 68.0% of the open conference papers are green open access
(

Figure 6). The difference shows within IEEE, which published
60.2% of the 2021–2025 output: 52.3% of its
journal publications are open, but only 15.0% of its conference
papers. Among journal publishers, MDPI (100.0%) and Frontiers
(100.0%) publish only open-access journals;
66.7% of the Springer Nature and
52.3% of the IEEE journal publications are open, but only
35.4% of the Elsevier ones.

Figure 7:Open-access share by funding status, source type and period: publications acknowledging an EU
research programme, publications with other funding only and publications without a funding
acknowledgement. Error bars: 95% Wilson confidence intervals (numbers of publications in the hover).

Funded publications are more often open access: in 2021–2025, 44.7% of the
funded and 38.1% of the other publications were open. The gap holds among
journal publications (65.7% against
54.4%) and within their two largest publishers (IEEE
55.0% against 47.5%,
Elsevier 40.5% against
25.6%). It is largest for publications acknowledging an EU
research programme: 78.2% of such journal publications were
open in 2021–2025, up from 63.9% in 2016–2020
(

Figure 7); Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe require open access to the peer-reviewed
publications of the projects they fund. Among conference papers only those acknowledging an EU research
programme stand out (26.6% open, against
12.0% with other funding only and
15.7% without an acknowledgement).

These are associations, not effects: funded and unfunded publications also differ in topic, venue and
collaboration, and the comparison does not control for these factors.

Funding data. Scopus extracts funder names and grant numbers from the acknowledgements of the papers.

How often are the School’s publications cited, how evenly are the citations spread across papers, which papers are cited most, and which kinds of papers attract more citations than comparable ones? This page answers these questions with the Scopus “Cited by” count of each of the 5,226 records, a snapshot taken on 2 November 2026. The counts include self-citations and only citations from documents indexed in Scopus.



Key findings

By 2 November 2026 the 5,226 publications had received 118,090 citations, a mean of 22.6 and a median of 6 per paper. The School’s h-index is 131 over all years and 88 for the papers published 2016–2025.

Citations are concentrated: the most-cited 1% of the papers hold 24.7% of all citations and the most-cited 10% hold 61.7% (all records, of mixed ages; within each publication year from 2000 to 2023 the most-cited 10% hold a median 57.8% of that year’s citations), while 10.8% of the papers published up to 2023 have not been cited.

Recent papers have had less time to be cited: papers from 2016–2020 average 29.0 citations, papers from 2021–2025 13.7, and 37.0% of the 2025 papers are still uncited.

Compared with papers of the same year and type (2000–2023), internationally co-authored papers are cited 21% above the School average, mainly those led by partners: the mean normalised score is 1.03 (95% CI 0.94–1.13) for international papers with an SECE first or last author and 1.56 (1.24–1.95) for those where SECE holds neither position. Counting only affiliations of co-authors who are not SECE authors, international papers score 1.22 (95% CI 1.09–1.36), so the association holds. Papers with a funding acknowledgement are cited 16% above the average; both differences remain when these characteristics and SECE leadership are considered together.

Journal papers are cited far more than conference papers: relative to all articles, reviews and conference papers of the same year (2000–2023), they score 1.58 against 0.29, a factor of 5.5.

The h-index is the largest number h such that h papers have at least h citations each. The School’s h-index is 131: 132 of its papers have been cited at least 131 times, but only 130 at least 132 times. The windowed h-indices count only the papers published in those years (with their citations up to 2 November 2026), so they are lower partly because they cover fewer papers and fewer years of citations. The mean is 3.8 times the median because a small number of papers are cited very often, as the next section shows.

Where do the numbers on this site come from, how were they produced, and how far can they be
trusted? This page describes the data sources and the processing pipeline, how affiliations were
linked to institutions and how accurate that linking is, the definitions used on every page, and the
known gaps in the data. All pages use the same 5,226 records dated
1981 to 2026, selected from a Scopus export taken on 2 November 2026.



Key findings

Scopus applies the search query across the affiliations of a record: 1,800 of
the 7,028 records it returned (25.6%) hold the query
words only in different affiliations and are left out. The records kept are precise:
5,219 of 5,226 (99.87%)
carry an affiliation of the School itself. Of the other 7, 2 give only a country as their
affiliation and 5 name AUTH only through other units of it, such as the Department of
Physics.

Leaving aside society memberships, 94.1% of the affiliation occurrences and
89.1% of those outside AUTH are linked to an organisation in the Research
Organization Registry (ROR). Outside AUTH the share drops to 68.0% in records
published before 2000.

On a fresh random sample of 240 affiliation strings, the matcher’s precision is
99.5% (95% CI 97.5–99.9%) and its recall 95.2%
(91.6–97.3%) with ROR v2.15. The legacy matcher it replaces scored 84.1% and
81.5% on the same strings.

Several fields are less complete in older records. The publisher is recorded for
29.1% of the records published before 2014 and for
99.0% of those from 2014 to 2025.
Funding acknowledgements appear on 18.2% of the 2011–2015
records and on 66.0% of the 2021–2025 records, a rise that may
reflect more funded research as well as more complete indexing.

Of the 13,025 affiliation occurrences (society memberships aside),
534 (4.1%, on
475 records) are affiliations outside AUTH held only by SECE
authors, that is, their own second affiliations; 325 of them are
abroad. Counting only affiliations of co-authors who are not SECE authors,
1,856 records are international instead of
1,953, and 46.7% instead of
50.6% of those of 2021–2025.

Partner, sector and country statistics depend on knowing which institution each affiliation names.
Scopus gives affiliations as free text, written differently from paper to paper, so the
7,344 distinct affiliation strings of the data set
(13,180 occurrences in records) were matched to ROR by a rule-based matcher that
prefers leaving a string unmatched to matching it wrongly:

Country first. The country is parsed from the end of the string (with aliases such as USA, UK,
Korea or Türkiye; Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan are kept separate), independently of the
organisation. The matched organisation’s country is used instead only when the string names no
country, or when the places in the string point to the organisation’s country.

Parts. The string is split at commas. Postcodes, street addresses, place names and the country
are set aside, and the remaining parts are ranked by how much they look like an organisation:
universities first, then institutes, hospitals and companies, and department or laboratory names
last.

Exact match of a normalised part (accents, abbreviations, word order, organisation words in
other languages) against every ROR name, alias and label, preferring organisations in the parsed
country.

Acronym match, only within the parsed country and only when the acronym is unique there.

Fuzzy match within the parsed country, requiring a shared distinctive word: a rapidfuzz
token-sort similarity of at least 89 (94 for parts without an organisation
word, 95 for strings whose country could not be parsed), or a part that differs
from a single organisation’s name only by place names or generic words. Department-level parts are
never fuzzy-matched, and fuzzy or acronym candidates that are universities or hospitals far from
every place named in the string are rejected.

Ignore and override. Strings that only state a society membership (such as IEEE or the
Technical Chamber of Greece) are ignored. Manual overrides, applied last, set the match of
17 strings.

Roll-up through ROR’s parent links to the top-level organisation, so that a research institute
counts with its parent organisation. Universities stay their own top level and are not merged into
university systems or federations.

Each string received one verdict per matcher, judged at the level of the top-level organisation:

correct: the right organisation, or a ROR parent or successor of it;

uncertain: the judge could not decide; left out of the metrics.

Publication, paper and record

One Scopus record of any document type; the pages use the three words interchangeably.

SECE affiliation

An affiliation string with a word starting with elec and a word starting with aristot, ignoring
case and accents. This mirrors the search query; 1,766 of the
7,344 distinct strings qualify.

SECE author

An author whose own affiliation text contains an SECE affiliation string. Scopus sometimes splits one
affiliation into an AUTH string and a department string, so an elec… unit that names no
institution, listed next to an aristot… string by the same author, also counts.
11,762 of the 22,180 author positions are SECE authors,
and every record with an SECE affiliation has at least one. The SECE first-, last- and corresponding-author shares build on these
flags; for the corresponding author, the affiliations in the correspondence address are tested with
the same rule.

AUTH affiliation

A string whose top-level ROR organisation is AUTH or, when it is unmatched, that names Aristotle
University (or AUTh).

Holder of an affiliation

An author of the record whose own affiliation text (the Scopus field Authors with affiliations)
contains the affiliation string. Holders are found with the same decomposition of the author’s text
as the SECE-author flag: a string that sits inside a longer string of the same author is held by that
author too, and an author whose text is empty holds nothing. An affiliation can have several holders,
some of them SECE authors and some not.

Dual affiliation and SECE-only affiliation

An author with a dual affiliation lists two or more affiliations on the same paper, such as an SECE
author who also holds a joint, adjunct or visiting position at another institution. Scopus lists all

How much does the School publish, how fast has its output grown, in which forms and in teams of
what size? This page counts the 5,226 Scopus records of the School of
Electrical and Computer Engineering (SECE) of AUTH dated from 1981 up to the export
of 2 November 2026. Each record counts once, however many co-authors it has (full counting),
except in the last section, which weights each record by its share of SECE authors.
2026 is a partial year: it is included in totals and marked in the charts of annual
counts, but left out of trends, growth rates, averages and shares by year or period.

This page looks at the people behind the School’s publications as a community: how many researchers publish with an SECE affiliation, how the community renews and how long newcomers stay, how concentrated output is, how often SECE researchers hold the first, last and corresponding author positions, and how they write papers together. Researchers are counted as Scopus author profiles, and an author counts as SECE on a paper when their own affiliation on that paper names the School (see 

Notes & caveats). All numbers are aggregates: the page shows no names, identifiers or per-person figures. Across the 5,226 records, 1,280 distinct profiles appear with an SECE affiliation at least once, in 11,762 SECE authorships (paper–author pairs).



Key findings

An average of 185 author profiles a year published with an SECE affiliation in 2021–2025, 2.1 times as many as in 2001–2005 (88). Output grew faster: 1,283 papers in 2021–2025 against 479 in 2001–2005 (2.7 times as many).

The community renews quickly, but few newcomers stay: of the 762 profiles whose first SECE paper appeared in 2001–2020, 48.6% published with an SECE affiliation again within five years and 20.9% in the fifth year after the first. The share coming back within five years fell from 56.5% for the newcomers of 2001–2005 to 40.3% for those of 2016–2020.

Output is concentrated: 50.5% of all profiles have a single SECE paper, while the most prolific tenth of the profiles active in 2021–2025 (46 profiles) appear on 84.6% of the School’s papers of those years.

An SECE author is first author on 56.1% of the papers of 2021–2025, down from 75.4% in 2001–2005. Part of the decline reflects the rise of international papers (from 21.7% to 50.6% of output), on which SECE authors are first less often: with the 2001–2005 rate of each collaboration type, the 2021–2025 mix alone gives 65.9%.

Teams grew mostly through co-authors without an SECE affiliation: their number per paper rose from 1.2 in 2001–2005 to 2.8 in 2021–2025, while the number of SECE-affiliated authors per paper rose only from 2.1 to 2.4.

What is the School’s research about, and how has its focus shifted? This page reads the publication titles, which every record has, so that one method covers all years: 5,222 titles from 1981 to 2 November 2026. The page lists the most frequent title terms, groups the titles into 12 research topics with a topic model and follows their shares and citation impact, compares the vocabulary of 2011–2015 with that of 2021–2025, and traces selected technologies over time. Titles only. The topics are read from the titles alone: every record has a title, so the same method covers all years, and the processed data the site is built from carry no abstracts or keywords. Titles are short and often name a method rather than the application (or the reverse), so term counts and topics describe emphasis, not an exact classification: a title about a neural-network method for antenna design counts for both terms.

Text preparation. The stop words are scikit-learn’s English list without the words that are engineering terms (system, side, thin, full, …) plus generic research words. Plural forms are merged by simple rules, spelled-out phrases are folded into their abbreviations, and translated titles in brackets are removed. These rules are approximate.

Topic model. TF-IDF of the single words and word pairs that occur in at least 5 titles (2,316 terms) and NMF from scikit-learn (initialisation nndsvda, random_state = 0), which gives the same result on every run for a given scikit-learn version and text preparation. Models with 10 to 15 topics were compared by topic coherence, the mean normalised pointwise mutual information (NPMI) of the ten top terms of each topic, from their co-occurrence in the titles. Coherence was highest with 12 topics (0.138) and decreased with fewer or more topics, to 0.059 with 10 and 0.052 with 15; the page uses 12 topics, the most coherent choice. Coherence and the topics themselves also shift when the text preparation changes slightly, so the choice also rests on inspection: with 12 topics the School’s main fields appear as separate, interpretable topics. Refitted on 10 random samples of 80% of the titles, the matching topics share on average 8.0 of their ten top terms with the full model, from 4.0 for Distribution grids & renewables to 9.6 for Control & robotics.

Topic names and assignment. The names were chosen by hand and are matched to the model’s topics through anchor terms; all 12 topics received a name. Topics are broader than their names: health-related titles, for example, count most often under Machine learning and edge-computing titles under Wireless & optical communications, and most titles that mention artificial intelligence count under Antennas & metamaterials, the topic in which the model gives that term its largest weight. Between 45.4% (Computational EM & photonics) and 86.4% (Energy management & storage) of a topic’s titles contain at least one of its 8 top terms; the others are assigned through further terms that the model links to the topic. Each title counts under its dominant topic, although for 34.4% of the titles the dominant topic carries less than half of the title’s topic weight. Fractional topic weights give similar changes between 2011–2015 and 2021–2025 (correlation 0.98 across topics). The three largest losses are then in Computational EM & photonics, Fading channels & diversity and Image & signal analysis.

Citation scores. As on 

Citation impact, the counts are Scopus “Cited by” values on 2 November 2026 (self-citations included), and the scores compare SECE papers with other SECE papers of the same year and type (articles and reviews together), not with the world. Means depend on a few highly cited papers (in every topic the median score is below the mean); the 2,000 bootstrap resamples show this uncertainty, and small topics tend to have wide intervals.

Rising and declining terms. The z-scores describe the difference between two periods; they are not significance tests and are not corrected for the 8,941 terms compared. With a prior of a quarter of the strength, 14 of the 15 rising and 12 of the 15 declining terms stay the same. Several declining terms belong to one line of work, silicon plasmonics (plasmonic, silicon, dielectric loaded, silicon plasmonic and plasmonic waveguides).

Selected technologies. Mentions are found in titles with regular expressions, and the abbreviations EV and PV are taken to mean electric vehicle and photovoltaic. The 3-year windows smooth year-to-year noise, but the early windows rest on few titles (76 in 1993–1995). The partial year 2026 is left out of all trends and periods.

Journals are identified by their Scopus source title; titles that share an ISSN (spelling variants and
renamed journals that kept an ISSN) count as one journal (8 titles merged),
listed under its latest title. Renamed journals that share no ISSN with their former title count as separate
journals, such as the IEE Proceedings and the IET journals that continued them.

Conference series. Edition names were reduced to a series by matching the conference acronym
(“EuCAP 2019”, “ICIP’02”), by removing years, ordinals, edition numbers and “Proceedings of”, and with a
list of aliases for series whose names vary between editions (host cities in IEEE PowerTech or the AES
Convention, renamed meetings such as the Metamaterials congress, parts of a joint meeting such as QELS at
CLEO) and for conferences that share an acronym with another series. A conference’s own workshop
proceedings count with it (ICC Workshops, for example), while a workshop or conference held in conjunction
with another meeting is a series of its own.
Where Scopus gives no conference name, the series is taken from the source title
if it names a meeting (such as a conference, symposium, congress or workshop) and is not a generic series like
Lecture Notes in Computer Science or CEUR Workshop Proceedings. The 76 other
conference papers without a conference name appeared in a journal or in a generic series; they cannot be
assigned to a series and count under their source title in the venue counts. The power, communications and antennas groups of the
leading series were assigned by hand from the series names.

Citations. Scopus “Cited by” counts on 2 November 2026, including self-citations. The normalised
citation score divides each paper’s citations by the mean of the School’s papers of the same year and
type (articles and reviews together), as on the 

Citation impact page; it is not a field-normalised indicator
against world averages, and a venue’s mean is sensitive to single highly cited papers.

Associations, not effects. Differences between publishers or venues reflect research field, team size,
collaboration and open-access status as much as the venue itself.

Diversity. The number of distinct venues grows with the number of papers. Rarefaction, the expected
number of distinct venues in a random draw of a fixed number of papers (Hurlbert, 1971), removes this size
effect when periods are compared.

Partial year. 2026 (records to 2 November 2026) is included in totals, in the tables
and in the yearly chart, but not in the period comparisons.
